# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–30 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing into summer and now winter. Year is 1830 (French Revolution year).
- **Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens," near Queen's Crawley); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall (Carbury Manor House, in Carbury parish); Carbury Chase; Beccles; Quenwick; Harrowgate.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (appointed administratrix). All other property muddled away in valueless shares.
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Arc (Chapters 27–30)
**Seduction and Enslavement of Jos Sedley**: At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos through calculated performance—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, falsely claiming virtuous past. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Within week, Jos became her "entirely slave." Changed habits; praised Dobbin constantly to Emmy; told her she behaved cruelly toward him. Lived in Brussels hotel in genteel manner with adjacent suite, carriage, entertainments.

**Dobbin's Opposition**: Called her "the little minx"; stormed at Jos. Amelia embraced Becky warmly and flung Dobbin an angry, scornful glance—the most unjust of her life. **Dobbin had spent fifteen years devoted to Amelia; she grew accustomed to trampling on him but did not wish to marry him—only to keep him.** Dobbin departed with haughty bow.

**Insurance and Death**: Jos effected heavy insurance; Dobbin procured prolonged leave, went alarmed. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle. Insurance company challenged payment, sent commission. Rebecca dared them to refuse, declared herself victim of "infamous conspiracy." Solicitors Messrs. Burke, Thurtell, and Hayes triumphed; £2,000 paid, split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (administratrix). **Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication with Rebecca.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declined to see her; receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham, where strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in works of piety, church attendance with footman, appears on all Charity Lists, has stalls at Fancy Fairs. Encountered Amelia and Dobbin at one fair; cast down eyes demurely.

## Amelia and William Dobbin's Resolution (Chapter 29)
**Becky's Revelation**: At Ostend, Becky revealed George Osborne was "selfish humbug, low-bred cockney dandy...who had neither wit, nor manners, nor heart." Produced letter: George "wanted me to run away with him—gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot." **"Dobbin forced him to keep his word."**

**Amelia's Transformation**: Emmy wept; internal struggle: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down...or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now.'"

**Marriage and Life**: Two mornings later at Dike, Amelia went to Dobbin "in dripping white bonnet and shawl...kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present at ceremony. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again." Dobbin quit service immediately, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to Mrs. Dobbin's child; they became great friends.

## Supporting Characters—Old
- **Glorvina O'Dowd**: Married Major Posky after his first wife's death. Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd advanced to Major-General; Lady O'Dowd lives in "great splendour at O'Dowdstown."
- **George Osborne (son)**: "Dashing young gentleman"; hunted and shot with Rawdon; at Cambridge; quarrelled with Rawdon over Lady Jane's daughter.
- **Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.** (young baronet): Lives at Queen's Crawley with Lady Jane and daughter; declined to see mother Rebecca.

## Lady Carbury and Family (Chapter 30)
**Character**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with son Felix and daughter Henrietta. **"The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was."** Devoted to children, especially Felix. Desperate to succeed; conviction that success comes not through good books but through inducing critics to praise them. No ambition to write good books; painfully anxious to write ones critics would praise.

**Workspace**: Back drawing-room (divided by permanently closed doors) is workspace for writing books and contriving systems to inveigle editors and critics. Rarely disturbed; admits no visitors except editors and critics.

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Mother spoilt him as boy and man; even during folly hardly ventured to stop him. Almost proud of his vices; delighted in hearing of his ruinous extravagance. Philosophy: "carpe diem"—never could see end of anything.

**Felix's Current Pursuit**: Considering courtship of Marie Melmotte (great heiress). Possesses two unpaid-for horses. Demands money from mother to maintain appearance in Grosvenor Square ("live a little up to the mark"). Mother provides funds though ill-afforded. Recently obtained money (amount unspecified); resolved not to repay mother's £20 loan or explain source. At Melmotte ball, **waltzes with Marie and studies words as lesson ("I do"), repeating them fairly well to send poor girl to bed with "sweet conviction that at last a man had spoken to her whom she could love."** Later left ball early to Beargarden—gambling devil hot within him despite fear of losing. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough and £400 from Miles Grendall through gaming.

**Henrietta Carbury** (daughter): Romance of life commenced. Cousin Roger Carbury (of Carbury Hall, head of Carbury branch) passionately in love with her; nearly forty years old. Paul Montague is another gentleman whom Henrietta has seen. At Melmotte ball, stood talking with Paul Montague while Lady Carbury endured evening.

## The Melmottes (Chapter 30)
**Augustus Melmotte, Esq.**: Arrived in London from Paris within last two years; previously M. Melmotte. Claims English birth though speaks native language fluently with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money,--though his character was perhaps worth but little."

**Madame Melmotte**: Said to have been Bohemian Jewess; admits to being foreigner, speaks very little English. Birthplace of daughter disputed: some say New York; Madame declares Paris. Jewish-looking appearance; considerable doubt whether Marie is actually her daughter.

**Marie Melmotte**: Spoke as Mademoiselle Marie; now speaks English well as foreigner. **Has begun forming own opinions; absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough** (bankrupt father, no income, ugly, vicious, ill-tempered). Had experience with Lord Nidderdale, who half-laughingly said he "might just as well take her for his wife." Now contemplating own happiness. **People saying if Sir Felix Carbury managed affairs well he might be the happy man.**

**Melmotte Wealth**: As affairs prospered, immediate disposition of Marie became less necessary; Melmotte reduced offers for suitors. Visible wealth certain: house, furniture, carriages, horses, servants with livery and powdered heads, black-coated servants, gems, presents. Two dinner parties daily—lunch at two o'clock, dinner at eight. Tradesmen "quite free of doubt"; "money in daily use" evident. Mystery about origins "rather pleasant as the money was certain."

## Roger Carbury of Carbury Hall
**Character and Standing**: Carbury of Carbury had never owed shilling he could not pay; father before him likewise. Orders to Beccles tradesmen not extensive; care taken goods neither overcharged nor unnecessary. Tradesmen consequently did not care much for him, though elders entertained ancient reverence for family. "Carbury of Carbury"—distinction of itself, which could not belong to Longestaffes, Primeros, or Hepworths of Eardly. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase (partly in Carbury parish, partly Bundlesham) belongs unfortunately in entirety to Bundlesham estate. Passionately loves Henrietta Carbury.
